title: Application Backlog
description:
Ordinary application work — defects, polish and small features that belong to no structural programme.

It exists so that this work is scheduled rather than deferred indefinitely. Everything else in the plan is a programme with a shape: a substrate being rebuilt, a feature being built, a harness being adopted. Work with no programme has no natural gate to hang from, and without a home of its own it loses every scheduling argument against work that does. Giving it an epic makes it contend on equal terms.

It is also where the plan absorbs load. Several of its launch units are deliberately wide — many independent sessions started together — because work with no shared file set and no shared reasoning is exactly the work that parallelises safely, and because running it that way is itself the test of whether the substrate carries concurrent sessions.

Expected to be permanent and never to empty.

title: Primary AI/Swarm Session adopt Agent Harness
description:
The Primary AI and its swarm workers stop assembling their own context and become consumers of the agent infrastructure.

Everything before this epic BUILDS that infrastructure — the registry, the instructions, the documents, the telemetry that measures what a context costs. This is the epic where the two things that actually run Darwin adopt it. Until they do, the infrastructure has no consumer that matters and its cost model is a hypothesis.

The ordering hazard is that the charters and the shared harness cannot be written before the layer they describe has settled: a charter written against a registry that is still being refactored documents a shape that will not exist, and a telemetry record shared by two domains cannot be specified before both domains agree on what a run is. That is why parts of this epic were deliberately left until late rather than written alongside the work they describe.

Adoption happens in three deliberate stages, and their order is a design decision rather than a convenience. The swarm session goes first because it is the consumer with the most rules and the least ability to argue with them: whatever classification survives contact with a real worker is the classification the other consumers inherit. The orchestrator goes second because it is the first consumer defined as much by what it must not do as by what it may, and a definition format that can only add capability would fail that test silently. The session a person sits in front of goes last because it is the least recoverable — a worker that boots wrong is repaired by the session above it, and there is no session above that one.

One decision is deliberately left open rather than answered here: whether an orchestrator that is itself a session should become the only way orchestration ever starts. Recording it as open is the point. It is the user's to make once there is something running to judge it against, and this plan must not foreclose it by building as though it were already settled.

title: Pipeline
description:
Pipelines-as-data: make a multi-requirement execution plan a first-class Darwin artifact the Primary AI can render, sequence and execute, instead of prose in a chat scroll.

The governing invariant is DERIVED, NEVER STORED. A step has no state column; its state is a pure function of its linked requirements' statuses, recomputed on every read. That invariant now extends to prose as well — a description carries purpose, and never a fact a query can answer.

The first phase built the artifact: the schema, the MCP API over it, the ordering and derivation engine, the table and visualizer views, the Primary's execution doctrine, a cost rollup, and an acceptance battery that replays every mutation class rather than asserting against a static fixture.

The second phase, Pipeline Orchestrator 2.0, replaced the per-gate watch-and-re-arm trigger model with one persistent engine, so that editing the plan became simply the next cycle's input. It also closed the defects that surfaced from executing this very epic with the first-generation tooling: a launch line that never fires for a late-linked requirement, an engine with no notion of work moving backward, grouping that would hand one epic's requirements to another epic's Primary, and a layout that renders brand-new work at the far left as though it ran first. Those defects were found by using the thing, which is the strongest argument available for having built it.

Design intent lives in memory/swarm-orchestration.md; the Primary's execution procedure in memory/swarm-orchestration-doctrine.md. The Pipeline Architect owns both.

title: Swarm Cloned Git
description:
Rebuild the swarm substrate so that a session is DISPOSABLE — its own clone of every repo it touches, provisioned from local mirrors, deletable with a single recursive remove and nothing anywhere left to reconcile.

The class of failure it eliminates is dual-path git access: one repository reachable by two different paths, two writers each convinced theirs is the real one. That produced actual repository corruption, and no amount of care in the calling scripts prevents it, because the hazard is in the topology rather than in any one command.

The rebuild is sequenced around two hard constraints, and both are about safety rather than convenience. Substrate surgery cannot begin while a worker is mid-lifecycle on the substrate being replaced, so the plan drains first and starts from zero in-flight work. And the machine-specific verifications need the user physically present at that machine, so they are their own units and the clone mechanism is proven per machine rather than assumed portable.

Nothing here is trusted because it was reviewed. A recorded all-passing baseline is what the cutover is measured against, the canaries run real lifecycles on the new substrate before the default flips, and the verification pass files defects rather than repairing what it finds — a verification that repairs has stopped being a verification. The canaries earned that: one of them caught a folder-trust dialog that silently blocked every clone session, a failure no review would have found because worktrees had been inheriting trust invisibly for as long as they had existed.

The Primary AI's own relocation belongs here and is the last thing to move. It is the one participant that cannot be migrated by a swarm session, since a session homed in the root being retired cannot survive its own retirement.

title: Mapping Aggregator Card
description:
Bring the aggregator concept to the mapping app: an always-first, toggleable card on the maps page that renders the concatenated GPS tracks of every selected ride the way the export map already does for one, and aggregates the photos discovered in each ride's time window onto that same map — so a season of riding reads as a single picture.

Alongside the card itself: a Mapping Architect owning the groomed mapping documents, the aggregator meta-pattern written up with both of its canonical implementations side by side, the epic planning pattern captured as a binding instruction, dev seed data so a human can review without reaching into production, validation with an explicit coverage-gap analysis, and a capstone that gates victory on the user's own review rather than on a green suite.

This epic replaces the old tracking-requirement convention: the plan itself is now the container, so nothing needs a placeholder row to hang work from.

title: Swarm Backlog
description:
Drain the approved Swarm backlog — groomed into three waves, serialized only where isolation genuinely demands it and parallel everywhere else.

The first wave is a set of independent fixes whose file sets were verified pairwise disjoint on 2026-07-31, so concurrent merges cannot conflict and the deploys that follow are lock-guarded. It covers the broken Primary closeout on the clone substrate — worth going first when capacity is limited, since until it lands no product-repo change can be closed out at all — removal of the automatic primary-sync hooks, a timestamp parsed as local time so dates render a day off, retirement of a hardcoded developer-machine path from the build config, and deriving swarm-start eligibility from the plan's own links rather than from each skill's private idea of what is launchable.

Two later additions are NOT covered by that disjointness verification, and it has not been re-run. The SQL database-target safety work is disjoint by inspection. The gate on running swarm skills under Haiku is not provably disjoint from the hook removal: if its chosen mechanism turns out to be a hook, both edit the same settings file. Verify before launching those two concurrently, or sequence them.

The second wave is the Windows/WSL machine cutover, with the user present at that machine. It can never be launched as a swarm session — the write-isolation guard blocks the paths it must touch, and a session homed in the root being retired cannot survive its own retirement. It has no dependency on the first wave and may overlap it; it is ordered second only because it gates the third.

The third wave is a single gateway write-path change that must follow the cutover, because that machine's verification battery leans on the same path and changing it underneath the battery would confound both results. That ordering is this epic's one hard serialization; everything else runs in parallel.

Provenance: three of these requirements were re-parented from other features, since a requirement carries exactly one feature link. Reversible if the prior placements are preferred.

title: Agent Polish
description:
Polish of the agent layer itself - the instructions, the guiding principles and the registry data that shape how every Claude session in Darwin behaves.

Distinct from adopting the agent harness, which is about the Primary and its workers CONSUMING that infrastructure. This epic is about the quality of what they consume: whether an instruction states its reason, whether a principle is written down or re-derived, whether the registry describes what is actually there.

Opened 2026-08-01 to give that work a home of its own. Expected to grow.

title: First Principles Pipeline
description:
Rebuild the pipeline layer on one containment chain, so that a plan's organisation and its execution are the same structure rather than two structures joined by a labelling tier.

The first-generation layer works, and it was proved by executing itself - which is the strongest argument available for having built it. What executing itself also proved is where the surface is larger than the problem. A step reaches its epic only through an intermediate tier whose whole job is to carry the label. The launch group is assembled out of steps, because steps were made narrow enough to need assembling. Ordering and state are derived twice, in two languages, kept honest by a corpus that can detect divergence but not prevent it. And a concurrency ceiling sits in the pipeline deciding something the swarm is better placed to decide.

This epic reduces that surface rather than extending it. An epic belongs to one pipeline and a step to one epic, so scope becomes a fact rather than an inference and the tie-breaks that exist only because it was inferred stop existing. The step becomes the launch unit and carries as many requirements as the work warrants, so launch overhead is paid once per unit of real work instead of once per requirement. Derivation gets one implementation. The intermediate tier and the launch group are removed outright, and the design says plainly what removing each one costs.

It comes up beside the existing layer rather than in place of it, because the existing layer is the plan that builds it. Both run at once on parallel tables, the older one is operated throughout, and it is eradicated only after the newer one has been watched doing the same job on the same work.

The hazard worth naming: this epic must use the very mechanism it deletes, because its own steps take their epic label through the tier being removed. That is not an obstacle to route around, it is the demonstration - nothing depends on that tier except the labelling path, and replacing the labelling path is exactly what containment does.

title: Catch-Up
description: Work that was approved or made ready to launch and then never sequenced by any plan, gathered so it runs under the same discipline as planned work instead of accumulating outside it. Its members answer to no common theme; what they share is that nothing was scheduling them, which is the condition this epic exists to end. It draws from more than one source of backlog, and the seats beneath it are what keep those sources distinguishable.

title: Bill's Polish #1
description: A round of polish chosen by the user rather than derived from a plan: the things that make the system unpleasant or untrustworthy to operate, gathered so they are worked deliberately instead of in the gaps between larger work. Its members share an origin, not a subject.

title: Pipeline 2.5
description: Container for Phase 3 work. Exists so Phase 3 requirements carry an epic of their own rather than one seated in another plan.
